blocks.text: Picture a photo on your phone. You never think of it as a giant grid of numbers, you just think of it as a picture. But the second you want to crop it, pull out just the red channel, or check one row of pixels for a scratch, you need a way to reach into that grid and grab exactly the piece you want. That reaching in is indexing and slicing, and it is one of the most used skills in all of NumPy.

blocks.alt: A NumPy array branching into picking one element, picking a slice, and a slice staying a view
blocks.caption: This lesson in one picture: pick one item, pick a range, and remember slices are views.

blocks.text: 1. Introduction

In the ndarray lesson you learned what an array actually is under the hood: a block of memory plus metadata like shape, dtype, and strides. Indexing and slicing are how you actually use that metadata day to day. Every time you write arr[3] or arr[1:4], NumPy is using shape and strides behind the scenes to figure out exactly which bytes to hand you back.

This lesson covers the basics: grabbing a single element, using the comma syntax for multiple dimensions, slicing with start, stop, and step, the ellipsis shorthand, and np.newaxis. By the end you will index into a realistic 3D image array without thinking twice about it.

blocks.title: What this lesson does not cover
blocks.content: Two more advanced indexing techniques exist: boolean masking, where you filter an array using a condition like arr[arr > 0], and fancy indexing, where you index with a list or array of positions. Both get their own dedicated lessons later in this module. Everything here is what NumPy calls basic indexing, and it behaves differently from those two in one important way you will see in section 5.

blocks.text: 2. Grabbing a Single Element
The simplest thing you can do with an array is ask for one item out of it. On a 1D array this looks exactly like indexing into a Python list, one integer inside square brackets.

code.content:
import numpy as np

arr = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40, 50])
print(arr[0])   # 10
print(arr[3])   # 40

blocks.text: 2.1 Positive Indices Count From the Front

A positive index counts from the start of the array, starting at zero. arr[0] is always the first element, no matter how long the array is. This is the same rule Python lists use, so if you already think in list indices, you already think in NumPy indices too.

code.content:
temperatures = np.array([21.5, 22.0, 19.8, 24.1, 20.3])
print(temperatures[0])   # 21.5, the first reading
print(temperatures[4])   # 20.3, the fifth reading

blocks.text: 2.2 Negative Indices Count From the Back

A negative index counts backward from the end of the array, and it starts at negative one, not negative zero. arr[-1] is always the last element, arr[-2] is the second to last, and so on. This is genuinely handy, since you rarely know the exact length of an array you are working with, but you almost always know you want its last item.

code.content:
print(temperatures[-1])   # 20.3, the last reading
print(temperatures[-2])   # 24.1, the second to last reading

blocks.alt: A five element array with positive indices counting from the front and negative indices counting from the back
blocks.caption: Positive indices start at 0 from the left, negative indices start at negative 1 from the right.

blocks.title: Out of bounds still raises an error
blocks.content: Reaching past either end of the array, whether with a positive index that is too big or a negative index that is too small, raises an IndexError. NumPy will not silently return garbage, it tells you the index is out of bounds for that axis.

blocks.text: 3. Multi Dimensional Indexing With the Comma Syntax
A 2D array has rows and columns, so grabbing one element needs two numbers, a row position and a column position. NumPy lets you pass both inside one pair of brackets, separated by a comma.
3.1 The Comma Form vs Nested Brackets

Plain Python has no comma syntax for indexing, so nested lists get indexed with two separate pairs of brackets, one for each level. NumPy arrays support that same nested style too, purely for familiarity, but it is not how you should actually write it.

code.content:
print(grid[1][2])   # also 6, same answer, different mechanism
print(grid[1, 2])   # the idiomatic NumPy way

blocks.alt: arr row 1 col 2 using comma syntax taking one fast step, versus arr row 1 then col 2 using nested brackets taking two slower steps
blocks.caption: Same result, very different amount of work happening underneath.

blocks.text: 3.2 Why NumPy Prefers the Comma Form

grid[1][2] actually happens in two separate steps. First grid[1] builds an entire new array object, a view representing row 1. Then [2] indexes into that temporary view to pull out the single number. You built and threw away an intermediate array just to get one value.

grid[1, 2] skips all of that. NumPy reads both numbers at once and uses shape and strides to compute the exact memory offset directly, in a single step, with no throwaway object in between. That is why the comma form is faster, and it is also why it is considered the idiomatic style, it says what you mean in one clear expression instead of two chained ones.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Style","How many steps","Temporary array built","Idiomatic"],"rows":[["grid[1, 2]","One","No","Yes"],["grid[1][2]","Two","Yes, for grid[1]","No"]]}

blocks.text: The comma form also scales cleanly. A 3D array is indexed as arr[i, j, k], a 4D array as arr[i, j, k, l], and so on, one comma separated position per axis, all resolved in a single lookup no matter how many dimensions you have.
4. Basic Slicing With Start, Stop, and Step

Instead of asking for one element, a slice asks for a whole range of them. The syntax is start:stop:step, where start is included, stop is excluded, and step controls how many positions to skip each time. Any of the three can be left out, and NumPy fills in a sensible default.

code.content:
arr = np.array([0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7])
print(arr[2:5])    # [2 3 4]      start 2, stop 5, default step 1
print(arr[:3])     # [0 1 2]      default start 0
print(arr[3:])     # [3 4 5 6 7]  default stop is the end
print(arr[::2])    # [0 2 4 6]    every second element
print(arr[::-1])   # [7 6 5 4 3 2 1 0]  a negative step walks backward

blocks.text: 4.1 Slicing a Single Axis

On its own, a slice on one axis works exactly the way it does on a plain Python list. What changes once you move to NumPy is that this same syntax applies independently to every axis of a multi dimensional array, which plain lists cannot do at all.

blocks.alt: An eight element array with a slice from index 2 to 5 highlighted, and a separate slice using a step of 2
blocks.caption: A slice on one axis pulls a contiguous or evenly spaced run of elements.

blocks.text: 4.2 Slicing Multiple Axes at Once
Just like the comma syntax for single elements, you can pass a separate slice for each axis, separated by commas. NumPy applies each slice to its own axis and combines the results into one sub array.

blocks.alt: A 2D grid sliced on rows from 0 to 2 and on columns from 1 to 3 combined into one sub grid
blocks.caption: Each axis gets its own slice, and NumPy combines them into a single rectangular sub array.

items: A missing slice for a trailing axis means take everything on that axis, so grid[0:2] is the same as grid[0:2, :].
You can mix a plain index and a slice on different axes, like grid[1, 1:3], which drops the row axis entirely and keeps a 1D slice of columns.
The same start, stop, step rules from a single axis apply independently to every axis you slice.

blocks.text: 5. Views Not Copies: The Slicing Gotcha

Here is the part that trips up almost everyone the first time. A basic slice, the colon style you just saw, does not hand you a fresh copy of the data. It hands you a view, a new ndarray object with its own shape, but pointing at the exact same underlying memory as the array you sliced from. This is the same view versus copy idea from the ndarray lesson, it just shows up here for the first time in the wild.

blocks.alt: An original array data buffer and a separate slice view object both pointing at the same shared memory block
blocks.caption: A slice is a new window onto the same numbers, not a fresh set of numbers.

code.content:
original = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40, 50])
view = original[1:4]
print(view)   # [20 30 40]

view[0] = 999
print(view)      # [999  30  40]
print(original)  # [ 10 999  30  40  50]   changed too, same memory

blocks.alt: Mutating one element through the view updates the shared memory block, which then shows up in the original array too
blocks.caption: Change the view, and you have quietly changed the original right along with it.

blocks.title: This is the exact gotcha from the ndarray lesson
blocks.content: The ndarray lesson section on view versus copy explained why this happens and showed .base and .copy(). The rule carries over directly here, any basic slice using the colon syntax is a view. If you need an independent array that will not leak changes back to the original, call .copy() on the slice, exactly as you did there.

code.content:
safe = original[1:4].copy()
safe[0] = -1
print(safe)       # [-1 30 40]
print(original)   # [ 10 999  30  40  50]   untouched this time

blocks.text: 5.1 Basic Indexing vs the Advanced Kinds

It is worth flagging this now so it does not surprise you later. Everything in this lesson, single elements, colon slices, ellipsis, and np.newaxis, is what NumPy calls basic indexing, and it always returns a view. Boolean masking and fancy indexing with a list of positions, both covered in their own lessons soon, are different beasts entirely, they always return a brand new copy, never a view. Same square brackets, very different behavior underneath.

blocks.text: 6. The Ellipsis Shorthand for Skipping Axes

Once an array has many dimensions, writing out a full slice for every axis you do not care about gets tedious fast. Say you have a 5D array and you only want to fix the very last axis to index 0, while keeping everything else untouched. Writing that out by hand means four colons in a row before your real index.

code.content:
tensor = np.zeros((2, 3, 4, 5, 6))
print(tensor[:, :, :, :, 0].shape)   # (2, 3, 4, 5), the tedious way
print(tensor[..., 0].shape)          # (2, 3, 4, 5), same result

blocks.text: Three dots, written as ..., stand in for as many full slices as are needed to fill out the remaining axes. NumPy figures out how many colons that expands to based on how many axes the array actually has, so the same ... works whether the array is 3D or 8D.

blocks.alt: A five dimensional array where an ellipsis silently skips over the middle axes so only the first and last axis are actually indexed
blocks.caption: The ellipsis expands to exactly as many full slices as it needs to, no more, no less.

blocks.title: Only one ellipsis per expression
blocks.content: You can only use ... once inside a single indexing expression, since NumPy would otherwise have no way to know how to split the remaining axes between two of them. One is all you ever need anyway.

blocks.text: 7. Inserting a New Axis With np.newaxis

Sometimes the array itself is fine, the numbers are all correct, but the shape is not quite what a downstream operation needs. np.newaxis, which is just a more readable name for None, lets you insert a brand new axis of length 1 exactly where you place it, without moving or copying a single number.

code.content:
vec = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
print(vec.shape)                    # (4,)

col = vec[:, np.newaxis]
print(col.shape)                    # (4, 1), a column vector

row = vec[np.newaxis, :]
print(row.shape)                    # (1, 4), a row vector

blocks.alt: A 1D array with shape 4 gaining a new length 1 axis after np.newaxis, becoming shape 1 by 4
blocks.caption: np.newaxis slots a length 1 axis in wherever you place it, the data itself never moves.

blocks.text: This turns out to matter constantly once you get to broadcasting, which has its own lesson right after this one. Reshaping a plain 1D vector into a row or column is often exactly the step needed to make two arrays broadcastable against each other.

blocks.title: Still just a view
blocks.content: Like a colon slice, indexing with np.newaxis returns a view, not a copy. You are only changing how the same underlying data is described, not duplicating any of it.

blocks.text: 8. Worked Example: Indexing Into a 3D Image Array

Let us put everything from this lesson to work on something concrete. A color photo loaded into NumPy is a 3D array shaped height by width by channel, where the channel axis holds three numbers per pixel for red, green, and blue.

code.content:
import numpy as np

image = np.random.randint(0, 256, size=(400, 600, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
print(image.shape)   # (400, 600, 3), 400 rows, 600 columns, 3 color channels

blocks.text: 8.1 Extracting a Single Channel

To pull out just the red channel, keep every row and every column, but fix the channel axis to index 0. That single number after the two colons is exactly the comma syntax from section 3, applied to a third axis.

code.content:
red_channel = image[:, :, 0]
print(red_channel.shape)   # (400, 600), a flat grayscale style plane

blocks.alt: A 3D image array with height, width, and channel axes, with the channel axis fixed to pull out a single 2D channel plane
blocks.caption: Fixing one axis and slicing full on the other two collapses a 3D array down to 2D.

blocks.text: 8.2 Extracting a Sub Region
Cropping the photo to a smaller rectangle just means slicing the row axis and the column axis, while leaving the channel axis untouched with a plain colon so every color stays.

code.content:
crop = image[100:200, 250:400, :]
print(crop.shape)   # (100, 150, 3), a 100 by 150 pixel crop, still full color

blocks.alt: A 3D image array sliced on rows and columns to pull out a smaller rectangular sub image, with all channels kept
blocks.caption: A crop is nothing more than a row slice and a column slice applied together, channels left alone.

blocks.title: Remember, this crop is a view
blocks.content: crop shares memory with image, exactly like section 5 described. Draw on it, modify a pixel in crop, and you have modified the original photo too. If you want to edit the crop safely on its own, call crop.copy() first.

blocks.text: 8.3 Extracting a Single Row of Pixels
To check one horizontal line of pixels across the whole image, all colors included, fix the row axis to a single index and leave the other two axes fully open.

code.content:
row_50 = image[50, :, :]
print(row_50.shape)   # (600, 3), every column in row 50, all three channels

blocks.text: Notice how naturally the comma syntax, slicing, and the view behavior all combined in this one example without you having to think about them as separate tricks. That is really the whole point of this lesson, these are not four unrelated features, they are one consistent way of addressing into an array.
9. Recap

blocks.content: {"headers":["Syntax","What it does"],"rows":[["arr[3]","Grabs a single element by position"],["arr[-1]","Grabs a single element counting from the end"],["arr[i, j]","Grabs one element from a multi dimensional array in one step"],["arr[2:5]","Slices a contiguous range on one axis"],["arr[::2]","Slices with a step, skipping elements"],["arr[0:2, 1:3]","Slices two axes at once"],["arr[..., 0]","Ellipsis fills in full slices for every unspecified axis"],["arr[:, np.newaxis]","Inserts a new length 1 axis for reshaping"]]}

items: A single integer index or a colon slice always returns a view that shares memory with the original array.
The comma syntax, arr[i, j] instead of arr[i][j], is both faster and the style every NumPy codebase expects.
The ellipsis saves you from writing out a wall of colons on high dimensional arrays.
np.newaxis reshapes without copying, which is exactly what broadcasting often needs.
Boolean masking and fancy indexing look similar but behave differently, they return copies, and they get their own lessons next.

blocks.title: Where to go next
blocks.content: The Reshaping and Broadcasting lessons right after this one build directly on np.newaxis and on the idea of shape. Boolean Masking and Fancy Indexing, later in this module, are where indexing stops being basic and starts letting you filter and reorder data by condition instead of by position.
